Three Points on a Parabola

Game: Move three dots on a curved line and watch how the straight lines through them meet.
How to play: Drag A, B and C along the curve, or use the sliders. Press Names or Tangents to show more of the picture, and Reset to put the dots back.

Look for the math

Three dots on one curve make a whole web of straight lines. Move them around: some lines stay side by side, and some crossing points sit exactly on other lines. That is the surprise here; there is no score to win.

The claim on the page

Put A, B, C on a parabola with a vertical axis. Draw AA', BB', CC' parallel to that axis, and let P = AB ∩ CC', Q = AC ∩ BB', R = BC ∩ AA'. Let tangents at B and C meet at M_A, those at C and A at M_B, and those at A and B at M_C. The page asks us to prove that M_A lies on PQ, M_B on PR and M_C on QR, and also that PQ, PR, QR are parallel to the tangents at A, B, C. This is a different claim from the neighbouring applet Greg Markowsky's Problem for Parabola: that one asks for an angle equality, ADC = BDC, for just two points and a point on the axis.

Where P, Q and R land

Write each point by its distance t from the axis, so its height is −t²/(4a) below the vertex. The chord joining parameters u and v has slope −(u+v)/(4a). Meeting that chord with the vertical through parameter w gives height (uv − uw − vw)/(4a). So P uses u=A, v=B, w=C, Q uses C, A, B and R uses B, C, A. Subtracting the heights of P and Q gives 2A(C−B)/(4a) over a horizontal step of B−C: the slope of PQ is −A/(2a), exactly the tangent slope at A. The same calculation works for PR at B and QR at C.

Where the tangent pairs meet

The tangent at parameter t has height −tx/(2a) + t²/(4a) at horizontal position x. Setting the tangents at v and w equal gives x = (v+w)/2 and height −vw/(4a). Put that x into the line PQ: the height comes out −BC/(4a), which is exactly M_A. Likewise M_B lies on PR and M_C on QR. The three claims are therefore one calculation: they are true for every choice of three distinct parameters. The logic test checks all of this over tens of thousands of triples, with the largest error under 1e−9 in exact arithmetic.

What the applet rounds

The old Java applet stored point heights as integers: Parabola(t) = t²/4/a with two whole-number divisions, then height − 40 − Parabola(t) − 40. It also stops redrawing when two slider values are equal, and its intersection routine calls a determinant below one "parallel" and leaves that point at NaN. This port keeps those behaviours, so the collinearity you see is only as good as the pixel rounding: across a step-10 grid of the whole slider range, 87% of settings put the three M points within 2 board units of their lines, while the worst case is about 16 units, and a slope differs by at most 0.13. A second, independent transcription of the bytecode agrees point by point. The live cut-the-knot page now shows only a Java warning; a 2012 Wayback snapshot embeds the applet the text describes.

Try A = 0, B = 80, C = −80, press Tangents and Names, then slide B towards A. Watch M_A run along PQ until the two sliders meet and the picture freezes.
